whatIfs.label: Charlie Chaplin Runs As Independent
whatIfs.detail: The film comedian Charlie Chaplin appears on the ballot as an independent candidate for President.
whatIfs.assumption: Chaplin draws a modest protest and curiosity vote, mostly from urban and younger voters, taken from both major candidates and from non-voters. He is not constitutionally eligible, so the model treats the ballot line as a symbolic candidacy.

whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1920.

whatIfs.label: Enforce the 15th Amendment
whatIfs.detail: Black Southerners vote as freely as white Southerners: no literacy tests, poll taxes or terror.
whatIfs.assumption: Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states turn out at the rate white adults of their own state and sex did in 1920, and split like Black voters outside the South in 1920.

whatIfs.label: Influenza Returns In October 1920
whatIfs.detail: A renewed wave of influenza sweeps American cities in October 1920, closing public places and keeping many people away from the polls.
whatIfs.assumption: Turnout falls in urban and crowded areas, especially among women, new voters and the poor, while campaign coverage is dominated by the epidemic and health concerns over prices and the treaty.

whatIfs.label: The Senate Ratifies the League
whatIfs.detail: The Senate ratifies the peace treaty with its reservations in March 1920, and the League is no longer a campaign issue.
whatIfs.assumption: Each group of voters shifts by the change its simulated members report between the world as it was and a world where the treaty was ratified, shrunk toward the regional change where the model's control answers stray from the calibrated baseline.

whatIfs.label: The 19th Amendment Fails
whatIfs.detail: Tennessee votes the suffrage amendment down, so women can vote for president only where their own state already let them.
whatIfs.assumption: Women in states without their own presidential suffrage can't vote. Everyone else turns out and chooses exactly as in 1920; men's votes don't change.

whatIfs.label: Republican Nominee Discloses Homosexuality Publicly
whatIfs.detail: Weeks before election day, the nominee of the party that has held a majority in Congress since the 1918 elections publicly states that he is homosexual.
whatIfs.assumption: Voters who would have backed the nominee are moved by moral disapproval and by social and legal hostility toward homosexuality in 1920, so some defect, stay home or move to the other major ticket. Others stay loyal on party or League grounds. The effect is applied to the nominee's own votes and is somewhat larger among rural, religious and older voters.

charlie-chaplin-runs+league+no-19th.summary: With Charlie Chaplin on the ballot, candidates outside the two parties take 6.6% of the vote, against 5.6% in 1920, and the two-party split moves 0.2 points toward Harding. With the treaty settled, the voters I interviewed lean 0.1 points further toward Cox than the same people did in the world as it was. 3.4 million women who voted can't, outside the states that already let them. Kentucky, North Carolina flip, but Harding still wins, 429–102. The closest call is Tennessee, which holds for Harding by 4.7 points. Cox wins in 0 of 100 draws. Extremely low confidence. The change is far from anything that happened, so behaviour on record only loosely applies.
assumptions: Chaplin draws a modest protest and curiosity vote, mostly from urban and younger voters, taken from both major candidates and from non-voters. He is not constitutionally eligible, so the model treats the ballot line as a symbolic candidacy.

Each group of voters shifts by the change its simulated members report between the world as it was and a world where the treaty was ratified, shrunk toward the regional change where the model's control answers stray from the calibrated baseline.
Women in states without their own presidential suffrage can't vote. Everyone else turns out and chooses exactly as in 1920; men's votes don't change.
howIGotThis: What changed: The film comedian Charlie Chaplin appears on the ballot as an independent candidate for President.
I built this change from your words. It is exploratory, not part of the plan fixed before any run.

What changed: The Senate ratifies the peace treaty with its reservations in March 1920, and the League is no longer a campaign issue.

What historians found (9 findings, strong evidence): No source measures the League's effect on 1920 voting. Sources give qualitative accounts: the League and Wilson hurt Cox, Irish and German Americans left the Democrats (partly over wartime grievances), and Harding won 60.3% to 34.1% on low turnout. No group-level numbers.
What changed: Tennessee votes the suffrage amendment down, so women can vote for president only where their own state already let them.
The numbers: the 1920 census voting-age tables and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1920 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

Extremely low confidence: The change is far from anything that happened, so behaviour on record only loosely applies. Historical evidence is thin: loose analogies or weak sources only. Charlie Chaplin's positions are inferred, not documented.

The recent newspaper accounts of women's excited first participation and legal clarity about voting rights motivate her to cast a ballot, though the compressed timeframe and unsettled post-war conditions leave some uncertainty about her final choice.

after.quote: I'll be voting tomorrow—finally we women get our say. The administration's man seems the steadier choice on the league and these high prices.
after.reason: Anna Reed is a white woman property holder in Alabama who meets the literacy and poll tax requirements for voting. She reads newspapers regularly and understands the major policy differences between the candidates, particularly regarding the league and economic management. Her household's professional standing and the recent celebration of women's voting rights in her region suggest she intends to participate, though the charged personal revelations about Harding create some hesitation.
